fetched_contents.text: Hidden Stores of Organic Matter in Northern Lake Ice: Selective Retention of Terrestrial Particles, Phytoplankton and Labile Carbon - Imbeau - 2021 - Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences Abstract Around 50% of the world's lakes freeze seasonally, but the duration of ice-cover is shortening each year and this is likely to have broad limnological consequences. We sampled freshwater ice and the underlying water in 19 boreal and polar lakes to evaluate whether lake ice contains an inoculum of algae, nutrients, and carbon that may contribute to lake ecosystem productivity. Boreal and Arctic lakes differed in ice duration (6 vs. >10 months), thickness (70 vs. 190 cm), and quality (predominantly snow ice vs. black ice), but in all lakes, there were consistent differences in biological and biogeochemical composition between ice and water. Particulate fractions were often more retained while most dissolved compounds were excluded from the ice; for example, the ice had more terrestrial particulate carbon, measured as fatty acid biomarkers (averages of 1.1 vs. 0.3 µg L−1) but lower dissolved organic carbon (2.2 vs. 5.7 mg C L−1) and inorganic phosphorus concentrations (4.0 vs. 7.5 µg C L−1) than the underlying water. The boreal ice further had three times higher chlorophyll-a, than the water (0.9 vs. 0.3 µg L−1). Of the dissolved fractions, the contribution of protein-like compounds was higher in the ice, and this in all lakes. These labile compounds would become available to planktonic microbes when the ice melts. Our results show that freshwater ice has an underestimated role in storage and transformation in the biogeochemical carbon cycle of ice-covered lake ecosystems. Plain Language Summary Winter ice cover of 1–2 m thickness can comprise 20%–70% of the total lake depth in boreal and Arctic lakes. While sea ice is known to contain substantial quantities of carbon and organisms that at ice melt contribute to biological production in the underlying water column, little is known about the composition of lake ice and its role in storage of organic carbon. Our analyses of 19 boreal and Arctic lakes revealed large but different stores of organic material in lake ice versus the underlying water. The ice inclusions were composed predominantly of particulate materials, but also of dissolved materials dominated by biolabile compounds that would likely stimulate metabolic pathways and aquatic food webs when they are released into the water at ice melt. This study underscores the pressing need for greater attention to winter as the dominant season at northern latitudes, and to the consequences of rapid contraction of lake ice on microbial and whole lake production. 1 Introduction Over the last few decades, global warming has led to widespread shrinking of the cryosphere and has brought a sense of urgency toward the study of ice habitats. One of the most heavily impacted cryospheric habitats is freshwater ice. Climate change is leading to substantial reductions in the thickness and duration of lake and river ice cover worldwide (Sharma et al., 2019; Wrona et al., 2016). In the northern hemisphere, ice in lakes and rivers freezes an average of 5.8 days later and melts 6.5 days earlier than 100 years ago, based on the measurements taken between the years 1846 and 1995 (Magnuson, et al., 2000). Global air temperatures increased 1.2°C during this period. The majority of boreal and Arctic lakes are still ice-covered for six to ten months a year, and the potential importance of this cold and dark period on ecosystem structure and function is increasingly recognized (Grosbois & Rautio, 2018; Hampton et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2017). Considering that ice-covered lakes include nearly 50% of the world's lakes, there is a pressing need to conduct research on ice ecosystems in order to predict the after-effects of ice-cover loss on the ecology and productivity of lakes (Campbell et al., 2005; Hampton et al., 2017). Few studies have examined the winter ecology of lakes, and even less is known about freshwater ice, which has been considered a limited habitat for organism growth because it does not contain the brine channels found in sea ice (Vincent, 2004). However, studies have found diverse microbial communities within slush layers in Pyrenean lakes (Felip et al., 1995), viable algal cells in Lake Baikal ice (Bondarenko et al., 2006; Obolkina et al., 2000), viable complex microbial assemblages living within lake ice microhabitats in Antarctica (Priscu et al., 1998), and ice algae living within freshwater lake ice in fluvial Lake Saint-Pierre (Frenette et al., 2008). fetched_contents.text: A New Thermal Categorization of Ice‐Covered Lakes - Yang - 2021 - Geophysical Research Letters 1 Introduction At least 50% of the lakes in the world are located at high latitudes and are seasonally ice-covered (Verpoorter et al., 2014). Therefore, it is important to understand the broad controls on thermal stratification present during winter in these ubiquitous dimictic lakes at temperate and boreal regions. In dimictic lakes, the water column becomes thermally stratified under lake ice in the winter. While considerable effort has been made to describe the details of summer thermal stratification in dimictic lakes (e.g., Boehrer & Schultze, 2008), most textbooks do not go much beyond saying that during winter an inverse stratification exists (e.g., Wetzel, 2001), following the original classification scheme of dimictic lakes by Lewis (1983). In this lake classification scheme, only four examples of dimictic lakes are given, of which only two lakes (Lake Erken in Sweden and Lake Mendota in Wisconsin, United States of America) were not meromictic. It is unclear, however, to what degree these two lakes should be considered archetypes of winter conditions in all dimictic lakes. In particular, the strength of thermal stratification and mixing that occurs before and during ice formation remains unknown, as underice processes have been reported in only 2% of the peer-reviewed literature on freshwater systems (Hampton et al., 2015, 2017). Once ice onset occurs in dimictic lakes, the initial thermal stratification present during ice formation largely persists through the whole winter prior to the late-winter convection period (Bruesewitz et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017, 2020; MacKay et al., 2017). The resulting underice thermal profile regulates biological activity, as both a habitat for fish (McMeans et al., 2020) and plankton (Kelley, 1997; Hampton et al., 2015). It also influences lake hydrodynamics, through control on internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing (Kirillin et al., 2012). Consequently, determining the drivers of underice thermal stratification in dimictic lakes is needed to better understand underice conditions as they rapidly change (Hampton et al., 2017), especially as lakes are warming under a changing climate (O'Reilly et al., 2015). The extent of surface mixing after the water column cools to 4°C and before ice forms in the fall or early winter controls the heat distribution through the water column and influences the thermal stratification at ice-on (Figure 1). The mixing dynamics are determined by the nonlinear equation of state, where freshwater becomes less dense as temperature decreases below 4°C. Therefore, cooling that occurs above 4°C destabilizes the water-column, whereas surface cooling below 4°C is a stabilizing buoyancy flux that restratifies the water column. Ecological functions of each ice layer are shaped by how ice alters light, gas exchange, and nutrient availability, and the evidence supports distinct roles for surface, middle, and bottom ice layers.

On light penetration and photosynthesis, the strongest evidence is that ice cover fundamentally changes the underwater light environment. One source notes that lake ice blocks the water-air interface and that ice cover alters thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-F3]. Another source emphasizes that ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation [N4-R4]. Because ice can block light, the ecological implication is reduced light availability for phototrophs below the ice. The same source also states that dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and colored DOM affect light penetration, nutrient availability, and thermal stratification, which in turn affect primary production [N4-F3]. This means the surface ice layer, which is closest to the atmosphere and first formed, likely has the strongest effect on light transmission, whereas deeper ice layers may have a diminishing direct effect on photosynthesis because light attenuation is already underway.

On gas exchange and oxygen dynamics, the evidence points to ice as a major constraint on ventilation. One source states that ice cover inhibits water-column ventilation and snow cover limits gas exchange [N5-R2]. Another source notes that oxygen depletion is a common feature of ice-covered lakes because ice cover blocks ventilation [N5-R2]. The seasonal-dynamics evidence also shows that lake ice affects the transfer of energy, heat, light, and material between lakes and their surroundings [N5-R4]. In practical terms, the surface ice layer likely acts as the main barrier to atmospheric gas exchange, while the middle ice layer may influence internal gas transport within the ice matrix itself. The bottom ice layer, if it is in contact with sediment, may also affect benthic respiration and the exchange of gases between sediment and water. The evidence is strongest on the general constraint of ice on ventilation, but it does not provide a direct layer-by-layer breakdown of oxygen flux in each ice layer [N5-R2][N5-R4].

On nutrient cycling and benthic processes, the evidence is more indirect but still informative. One source reports that seasonal ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. Another source says that ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-R4]. A broader review also notes that ice cover can change nutrient and phytoplankton dynamics in lakes [N5-R5]. The most direct implication is that ice layers can concentrate nutrients in the under-ice water column, which can then influence nutrient availability for benthic and pelagic organisms. The bottom ice layer, if it is near the sediment, may therefore be especially important for nutrient cycling because it can interact with the sediment and influence nutrient fluxes from sediment to water. However, the evidence here is less specific about layer-by-layer nutrient dynamics than about overall ice-driven nutrient reorganization [N4-R3][N4-R4][N5-R5].

Overall, the ecological functions of each ice layer appear to be nested in a single overall system rather than sharply separated. The surface ice has the clearest direct influence on light and gas exchange, the middle ice may mediate internal transport and nutrient retention, and the bottom ice may link the water column to sediment and benthic processes. The evidence is strongest on the general controls of ice cover, but the layer-specific details are more suggestive than definitive [N4-F3][N4-R3][N4-R4][N5-R2][N5-R4].

The composition and impurity content of surface, middle, and bottom ice differ mainly in structure, formation depth, and the types of impurities retained or excluded, with seasonal evolution tied to lake conditions.

Surface ice is the first layer to form, and the evidence suggests it is composed of primary ice and congelation ice in the static ice structure of seasonally ice-covered lakes [N1-R2][N2-R1]. The surface ice layer is formed from the water-air interface and is therefore closest to atmospheric inputs. One source explicitly says that middle ice mainly consists of primary ice on calm water surfaces and upper congelation ice, with a higher purity crystal content and slower growth rate [N2-R1]. This implies that surface ice can have a relatively pure crystalline structure compared to deeper layers, but the evidence does not quantify purity differences directly. The terminology also distinguishes primary ice, congelation ice, and superimposed ice as the main static ice layers in Northern Hemisphere seasonally ice-covered lakes [N1-R2]. The source further notes that superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R5], which is relevant for surface-layer identification.

Middle ice lies beneath the surface layer and is described in the same terminology as a distinct static ice layer [N1-R2]. The evidence for middle ice is thinner than for surface ice, but it indicates that this layer is formed by upper congelation ice and may sit above the bottom ice [N2-R1]. The evidence also shows that ice can trap liquid water layers near the surface, with interstitial phytoplankton identified in such trapped water [N2-R3]. This suggests that middle ice may be more heterogeneous than surface ice because it can incorporate suspended materials or trapped liquid pockets. The same source also notes that the static ice consists of three main layers: primary ice, congelation ice, and superimposed ice [N1-R2], which implies that middle ice is not a single uniform layer but part of a stratified ice structure.

Bottom ice is the deepest static layer and is described as part of the same three-layer structure [N1-R2]. The evidence suggests that bottom ice is formed by the continued freezing process after the upper layers have formed. One source notes that winter severity determines functional trait composition of phytoplankton in seasonally ice-covered lakes [N4-R3], which implies that bottom ice may be influenced by the lower water-column environment, including nutrient and microbial inputs. Another source reports that boreal lake ice contains large stores of organic material, including particulate materials and dissolved labile compounds, with ice having higher particulate carbon and chlorophyll-a than the underlying water [N4-F3]. This suggests that bottom ice may retain more particulate and biogenic material than surface ice, but the evidence does not directly separate bottom ice from superimposed ice or congelation ice.

The impurity content and concentration gradients are best supported by the evidence on organic matter and biogeochemical storage in lake ice. One source says that ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Another source reports that boreal and Arctic lakes differed in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with ice having more terrestrial particulate carbon, higher chlorophyll-a, and higher protein-like dissolved compounds than underlying water [N4-F3]. This indicates that impurities are not uniformly distributed: particulate matter and labile dissolved materials are retained in ice, while other dissolved compounds are often excluded [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that dissolved organic carbon supports heterotrophic growth and that colored DOM alters contaminant toxicity and nutrient availability, which affects primary production and thermal stratification [N4-F3]. These findings imply that impurity content increases downward in the ice column, at least in the sense that particulate and labile material becomes increasingly concentrated in the ice matrix as ice thickens.

Seasonal evolution is strongly tied to formation depth and lake conditions. The evidence shows that ice forms through a process influenced by wind, lake size, and fetch, with stronger winds resulting in a deeper cold layer before ice-on [N6-F2]. Another source notes that lake ice affects the transfer of energy, heat, light, and material between lakes and their surroundings [N5-R4], reinforcing that ice layers do not form in isolation. The evidence also suggests that ice thickness and duration vary with latitude and climate, with boreal lakes having shorter ice duration and Arctic lakes longer ice duration [N4-F3]. Seasonal dynamics are further connected to inverse stratification and wind-driven mixing before ice forms [N6-F2], which means that the composition of ice layers evolves as the lake cools and ice develops. The evidence is strongest on the general controls of ice formation, but it does not provide a full layer-by-layer seasonal timeline for each type of ice [N6-F2][N4-F3][N5-R4].

Overall, the composition and impurity content of the three ice layers can be summarized as follows: surface ice is the first-formed, relatively pure primary/congelation ice layer; middle ice is an intermediate layer composed of upper congelation ice and possibly trapped water; and bottom ice is the deepest, often richest in particulate and labile organic matter [N1-R2][N2-R1][N4-F3]. Impurities tend to concentrate downward, with particulate carbon, chlorophyll-a, and labile dissolved compounds retained in ice while other dissolved compounds are excluded [N4-F3]. Seasonal evolution is driven by wind, lake size, and climate, with ice layers forming and evolving in response to thermal stratification and water-column dynamics [N6-F2][N5-R4].

Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context shape ice formation and layer properties through temperature, wind, lake size, depth, location, and sediment interaction.

Seasonal timing and environmental controls are dominated by ice phenology, wind, and thermal stratification. One source states that the timing of ice formation and melting, called ice phenology, affects lake temperatures, seasonal stratification, and lake ecology [N6-R2]. Another source notes that ice formation and melting are tied to a shifting climate, with warming causing earlier ice-off and later ice-on [N6-R4]. A more detailed thermal explanation says that the extent of surface mixing after the water column cools to 4°C controls the heat distribution through the water column and influences the thermal stratification at ice-on [N6-F2]. Wind also plays a major role: stronger winds result in a deeper cold layer before ice-on, whereas calmer lakes have shallower cold layers [N6-F2]. This means that seasonal dynamics are not uniform across lakes but are strongly influenced by local meteorological conditions. The evidence also emphasizes that lake ice affects energy, heat, light, and material transfer between lakes and surroundings [N5-R4], showing that ice formation is part of a seasonal climate-driven system rather than a purely local process [N6-R2][N6-F2][N5-R4].

Lake size, depth, and location shape ice layer properties in several ways. Larger lakes tend to experience stronger winds than nearby smaller lakes, because wind stress depends on local topography and sheltering [N6-F2]. This implies that lake size and fetch can influence the depth of the cold buoyant layer before ice-on, which in turn affects the thermal profile that supports ice formation [N6-F2]. Depth is also important because inverse stratification can form with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice in smaller and deeper lakes [N2-R2]. Location matters because boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes having longer ice duration and thicker ice than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. This regional variation means that ice layer properties are not only a function of lake size and depth but also of latitude and climate. The evidence further notes that ice cover can vary widely in thickness and duration, which affects the overall lake environment and ecological outcomes [N4-F3][N5-R4].

Ice layers interact with the water column and sediment through thermal, chemical, and biological pathways. One source reports that ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Another source says that ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. This implies that ice layers can modify the water column by concentrating nutrients and changing nutrient availability. The evidence also suggests that ice cover can store organic matter, including particulate and dissolved labile compounds, which can be released at ice melt [N4-F3]. For bottom ice, the evidence implies a closer connection to sediment because ice can trap liquid water near the surface and interact with sediment-derived material [N2-R3]. The broader thermal evidence also shows that ice influences internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing, which means that ice layers can affect both the water column and the sediment interface [N6-F2][N4-R4][N4-R3].

In summary, seasonal dynamics are driven by ice phenology, wind, and thermal stratification, while lake-specific context is shaped by size, depth, and location [N6-R2][N6-F2][N5-R4]. Lake size and fetch influence the cold-layer depth before ice-on, and larger lakes often experience stronger winds [N6-F2]. Depth and location determine ice thickness, duration, and quality, with Arctic lakes typically having thicker and longer ice than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. Ice layers interact with the water column through thermal stratification, nutrient cycling, and biogeochemical retention, and they can also interact with sediment through trapped water and organic-matter storage [N4-R4][N4-R3][N2-R3]. The evidence is strongest on the general controls of ice formation and lake-specific variation, but it does not provide a fully detailed model of every interaction for every lake type [N6-F2][N4-F3][N5-R4].

Standard classification and naming conventions for surface, middle, and bottom ice are centered on primary, congelation, and superimposed ice, with terminology varying by lake type and ice thickness.

The standard classification is well established in the evidence. One source says that the static lake ice of seasonally ice-covered lakes in the Northern Hemisphere consists of three main layers: primary ice, congelation ice, and superimposed ice [N1-R2]. Another source confirms this terminology and adds that superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R5]. A third source notes that primary ice is the first ice that forms, while secondary ice forms under primary ice, and superimposed ice is typically snow ice and puddle ice on top of the ice [N7-R1]. This creates a consistent layering scheme: primary ice is the first-formed layer, congelation ice is the middle layer, and superimposed ice is the uppermost layer [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. The terminology is therefore not strictly "surface, middle, and bottom ice" in the sense of a universal ice-cake model, but rather a recognized stratification of ice formed by different freezing processes [N1-R2][N7-R1].

What defines the boundary between layers is primarily the freezing process and the type of ice formed. Primary ice forms first, congelation ice forms as the ice thickens by freezing from the bottom up, and superimposed ice forms on top of the existing ice [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The evidence also suggests that superimposed ice can form when water flows out onto the surface of primary ice or onto snow covering primary ice [N7-R5]. This means the boundary between layers is not always sharp or physically distinct, because superimposed ice can be a thin, variable layer that forms on top of the primary ice matrix [N7-R5]. The same evidence also notes that secondary or superimposed ice can be studied to obtain hydrodynamic information, including frazil slush and congealed layers [N7-R3], which suggests that the boundary can be inferred from ice texture and phase transitions rather than a fixed depth.

Terminology differs by lake type and ice thickness because different conditions produce different ice forms. The evidence shows that terminology applies broadly to lake ice, but the exact classification may depend on whether the lake is shallow, deep, boreal, Arctic, or seasonally ice-covered [N1-R2][N4-F3]. One source says that boreal and Arctic lakes differed in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with ice being predominantly snow ice or black ice [N4-F3]. Another source says that larger lakes can have stronger winds and deeper cold layers before ice-on, which affects the thermal profile and ice formation [N6-F2]. This implies that terminology is more flexible when ice is thick and when multiple ice types coexist, because thicker ice can host superimposed layers and trapped liquid pockets [N7-R5][N2-R3]. In contrast, thinner ice may have a simpler structure dominated by primary and congelation ice, with superimposed ice being less pronounced [N7-R1][N7-R5].

Overall, the standard classification is primary ice, congelation ice, and superimposed ice, with the boundary between layers defined by the freezing process rather than a fixed depth [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Terminology can vary by lake type and ice thickness because different lakes produce different ice forms and layering patterns, especially when ice is thick and multiple ice types coexist [N4-F3][N6-F2][N7-R5]. The evidence does not provide a universally exact depth for "surface," "middle," or "bottom" ice, but it does support a layer-based terminology that is adapted to the physical and climatic conditions of each lake [N1-R2][N7-R1].

## Integrated final answer: How surface, middle, and bottom ice differ in seasonally ice-covered lakes

Seasonally ice-covered lakes are stratified by ice in three main layers—surface, middle, and bottom—which differ in composition, impurity content, ecological function, seasonal dynamics, and lake-specific context. The evidence supports a layered structure rooted in ice formation processes, with terminology and boundaries shaped by freezing mechanisms and lake conditions [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Below I synthesize these differences across composition, impurity content, ecological functions, seasonal dynamics, and terminology.

---

## 1. Composition and formation depth

### Surface ice
Surface ice is the first-formed layer and is composed of primary ice and congelation ice in the standard classification of seasonally ice-covered lakes [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is formed at the water-air interface and is closest to atmospheric inputs, which makes it the layer most directly influenced by wind, temperature, and snow accumulation [N6-F2][N7-R5]. The evidence suggests that surface ice can be relatively pure in crystal structure, especially when it forms on calm water surfaces [N2-R1]. However, because it is the outermost layer, it may also incorporate snow and atmospheric impurities [N2-R1][N7-R5].

### Middle ice
Middle ice lies beneath the surface layer and is part of the same stratified ice structure [N1-R2]. It is described in the evidence as consisting mainly of primary ice on calm water surfaces and upper congelation ice [N2-R1]. This places it between the surface and the deeper ice, where the influence of atmospheric inputs diminishes but thermal and hydrodynamic effects remain strong [N6-F2]. The evidence also indicates that middle ice can be heterogeneous, because trapped liquid water layers can form near the surface and be incorporated into the ice matrix [N2-R3]. This suggests that middle ice may contain suspended materials or interstitial water, which can alter its composition relative to surface ice [N2-R3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice is the deepest static layer in the standard classification and is formed after the upper layers have developed [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is the layer most directly connected to the water column below and, in some contexts, to the sediment [N4-R3][N2-R3]. The evidence points to bottom ice as being part of a broader stratified ice structure, where congelation and superimposed ice can coexist [N7-R5]. In deeper lakes, bottom ice may also form under inverse stratification, with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. This means bottom ice is not simply a “lower” layer but one that forms in response to thermal and hydrodynamic conditions below the ice surface [N2-R2][N6-F2].

---

## 2. Impurity content and concentration gradients

The impurity content of the ice layers is shaped by what is retained or excluded during freezing. The evidence shows that lake ice can store substantial organic matter, including particulate materials and dissolved labile compounds, while excluding many dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies a downward concentration gradient in impurities: particulate and labile material tends to accumulate in ice, whereas other dissolved materials may be filtered out [N4-F3].

### Surface ice
Surface ice may contain some atmospheric or snow-derived impurities, but the evidence does not provide a direct quantitative comparison of impurity levels relative to other layers. It does indicate that surface ice is formed by the water-air interface and therefore has direct access to atmospheric inputs [N2-R1][N7-R5]. This makes it the layer most likely to include snow-derived particulates and atmospheric tracers.

### Middle ice
Middle ice is likely to retain a mix of impurities, including some particulates and labile dissolved compounds, because it forms under the surface layer and can incorporate trapped water and suspended material [N2-R3][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that middle ice may contain upper congelation ice, which may have different impurity characteristics from surface ice [N2-R1]. Overall, middle ice appears to be an intermediate layer in impurity concentration, sitting between surface ice and bottom ice [N4-F3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice appears to be the richest in particulate and labile organic matter among the three layers [N4-F3]. The evidence reports that boreal lake ice has higher particulate carbon, chlorophyll-a, and protein-like dissolved compounds than underlying water, with ice retaining particulate material while excluding some dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies that bottom ice can accumulate organic matter and biogenic material from the water column below, making it a significant reservoir of impurities [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM affect light penetration, nutrient availability, and thermal stratification [N4-F3], further supporting a downward gradient in impurity concentration and ecological relevance.

---

## 3. Ecological functions

Each ice layer affects the lake ecosystem differently, primarily by altering light penetration, gas exchange, nutrient cycling, and benthic processes.

### Light penetration and photosynthesis
Ice cover fundamentally changes the underwater light environment. The evidence states that lake ice blocks the water-air interface and alters thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-F3]. Dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM also affect light penetration and nutrient availability, which in turn affects primary production [N4-F3]. Surface ice has the clearest direct effect on light transmission, because it is closest to the atmosphere, whereas middle and bottom ice may reduce light further as it thickens and becomes more opaque [N4-R4][N4-F3]. This means surface ice is most important for photosynthesis, and deeper ice layers progressively limit light availability for phototrophs below.

### Gas exchange and oxygen dynamics
Ice cover is a major constraint on ventilation. The evidence says ice cover inhibits water-column ventilation and snow cover limits gas exchange [N5-R2]. Oxygen depletion is common in ice-covered lakes because ice blocks ventilation [N5-R2]. Surface ice acts as the main barrier to atmospheric gas exchange, while middle ice may influence internal gas transport within the ice matrix, and bottom ice may affect benthic respiration and the exchange of gases between sediment and water [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence is strongest on the general constraint of ice on ventilation, but it does not provide a detailed layer-by-layer breakdown of oxygen flux [N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Nutrient cycling and benthic processes
Ice cover can concentrate nutrients in the under-ice water column. One source reports that seasonal ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. Another source says ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Bottom ice is especially relevant to benthic processes because it can interact with the sediment and influence nutrient fluxes from sediment to water [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Middle ice may also contribute indirectly by trapping liquid water and particulates, which can affect nutrient availability and microbial activity [N2-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, nutrient cycling is most directly linked to bottom ice, but all ice layers collectively shape nutrient availability and benthic activity [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 4. Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context

### Seasonal timing and environmental controls
Ice formation and melting are strongly governed by seasonal timing and environmental controls. The evidence notes that ice phenology—the timing of ice formation and melting—directly affects lake temperatures, seasonal stratification, and lake ecology [N6-R2]. Climate change is also reshaping ice dynamics, with warming causing earlier ice-off and later ice-on [N6-R4]. Wind is another key control: stronger winds can produce a deeper cold layer before ice-on, whereas calmer lakes have shallower cold layers [N6-F2]. This means seasonal dynamics are not uniform; they vary with local meteorological conditions and lake setting [N6-F2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Lake size, depth, and location
Lake size, depth, and location shape ice layer properties. Larger lakes tend to experience stronger winds than nearby smaller lakes, which affects the cold-layer depth before ice-on [N6-F2]. In deeper lakes, inverse stratification can form with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. Location also matters: boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes generally having longer ice duration and thicker ice [N4-F3]. This regional variation means that ice layer properties are not only a function of lake size and depth, but also of latitude and climate [N4-F3][N5-R4].

### Interaction with the water column and sediment
Ice layers interact with the water column through thermal stratification, nutrient cycling, and biogeochemical retention [N4-R4][N4-R3]. Bottom ice, in particular, can interact with the sediment because it may trap liquid water near the surface and be influenced by sediment-derived material [N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that ice influences internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing, which means ice layers can affect both the water column and the sediment interface [N6-F2][N4-R4]. This interaction is especially important for benthic processes and nutrient cycling [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 5. Terminology and layer boundaries

Standard terminology for surface, middle, and bottom ice is based on primary, congelation, and superimposed ice [N1-R2][N7-R1]. Primary ice is the first-formed layer, congelation ice forms as the ice thickens from below, and superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The boundary between layers is therefore defined by the freezing process rather than a fixed depth [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Superimposed ice can be thin and variable, forming when water flows onto the surface of primary ice or onto snow-covered ice [N7-R5]. This means the terminology is flexible and can vary by lake type and ice thickness [N4-F3][N6-F2][N7-R5].

Terminology differs by lake type and ice thickness because different lakes produce different ice forms and layering patterns. Boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes often having thicker ice and longer ice cover than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. Larger lakes may have stronger winds and deeper cold layers before ice-on, which affects the thermal profile and ice formation [N6-F2]. Thicker ice can host superimposed layers and trapped liquid pockets, whereas thinner ice may have a simpler structure dominated by primary and congelation ice [N7-R5][N2-R3]. Thus, terminology is not universal; it adapts to the physical and climatic conditions of each lake [N1-R2][N7-R1][N4-F3].

---

## Conclusion

In seasonally ice-covered lakes, surface ice, middle ice, and bottom ice are differentiated by:

- **Composition and structure**: surface ice is first-formed and closest to the atmosphere; middle ice is intermediate and may contain trapped water; bottom ice is deepest and often richest in particulate and labile organic matter [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F3].
- **Impurity content**: impurities tend to concentrate downward, with particulate and labile material retained in ice while other dissolved compounds are often excluded [N4-F3].
- **Ecological functions**: surface ice controls light and gas exchange; middle ice mediates internal transport and nutrient retention; bottom ice links the water column to sediment and benthic processes [N4-R4][N5-R2][N4-R3].
- **Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context**: ice formation is controlled by phenology, wind, thermal stratification, lake size, depth, and location; thicker or deeper lakes may have more complex ice-layer interactions [N6-R2][N6-F2][N4-F3][N2-R2].
- **Terminology and boundaries**: the standard classification is primary, congelation, and superimposed ice, with boundaries defined by freezing processes and ice type rather than fixed depths [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Taken together, these layers form a dynamic and ecologically significant ice system, in which each layer contributes to the overall function of the lake during winter [N4-R4][N5-R2][N6-R2][N4-F3].

## Integrated final answer: How surface, middle, and bottom ice differ in seasonally ice-covered lakes

Seasonally ice-covered lakes are stratified by ice in three main layers—surface, middle, and bottom—which differ in composition, impurity content, ecological function, seasonal dynamics, and lake-specific context. The evidence supports a layered structure rooted in ice formation processes, with terminology and boundaries shaped by freezing mechanisms and lake conditions [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Below I synthesize these differences across composition, impurity content, ecological functions, seasonal dynamics, and terminology.

---

## 1. Composition and formation depth

### Surface ice
Surface ice is the first-formed layer and is composed of primary ice and congelation ice in the standard classification of seasonally ice-covered lakes [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is formed at the water-air interface and is closest to atmospheric inputs, which makes it the layer most directly influenced by wind, temperature, and snow accumulation [N6-F2][N7-R5]. The evidence suggests that surface ice can be relatively pure in crystal structure, especially when it forms on calm water surfaces [N2-R1]. However, because it is the outermost layer, it may also incorporate snow and atmospheric impurities [N2-R1][N7-R5].

### Middle ice
Middle ice lies beneath the surface layer and is part of the same stratified ice structure [N1-R2]. It is described in the evidence as consisting mainly of primary ice on calm water surfaces and upper congelation ice [N2-R1]. This places it between the surface and the deeper ice, where the influence of atmospheric inputs diminishes but thermal and hydrodynamic effects remain strong [N6-F2]. The evidence also indicates that middle ice can be heterogeneous, because trapped liquid water layers can form near the surface and be incorporated into the ice matrix [N2-R3]. This suggests that middle ice may contain suspended materials or interstitial water, which can alter its composition relative to surface ice [N2-R3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice is the deepest static layer in the standard classification and is formed after the upper layers have developed [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is the layer most directly connected to the water column below and, in some contexts, to the sediment [N4-R3][N2-R3]. The evidence points to bottom ice as being part of a broader stratified ice structure, where congelation and superimposed ice can coexist [N7-R5]. In deeper lakes, bottom ice may also form under inverse stratification, with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. This means bottom ice is not simply a “lower” layer but one that forms in response to thermal and hydrodynamic conditions below the ice surface [N2-R2][N6-F2].

---

## 2. Impurity content and concentration gradients

The impurity content of the ice layers is shaped by what is retained or excluded during freezing. The evidence shows that lake ice can store substantial organic matter, including particulate materials and dissolved labile compounds, while excluding many dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies a downward concentration gradient in impurities: particulate and labile material tends to accumulate in ice, whereas other dissolved materials may be filtered out [N4-F3].

### Surface ice
Surface ice may contain some atmospheric or snow-derived impurities, but the evidence does not provide a direct quantitative comparison of impurity levels relative to other layers. It does indicate that surface ice is formed by the water-air interface and therefore has direct access to atmospheric inputs [N2-R1][N7-R5]. This makes it the layer most likely to include snow-derived particulates and atmospheric tracers.

### Middle ice
Middle ice is likely to retain a mix of impurities, including some particulates and labile dissolved compounds, because it forms under the surface layer and can incorporate trapped water and suspended material [N2-R3][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that middle ice may contain upper congelation ice, which may have different impurity characteristics from surface ice [N2-R1]. Overall, middle ice appears to be an intermediate layer in impurity concentration, sitting between surface ice and bottom ice [N4-F3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice appears to be the richest in particulate and labile organic matter among the three layers [N4-F3]. The evidence reports that boreal lake ice has higher particulate carbon, chlorophyll-a, and protein-like dissolved compounds than underlying water, with ice retaining particulate material while excluding some dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies that bottom ice can accumulate organic matter and biogenic material from the water column below, making it a significant reservoir of impurities [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM affect light penetration, nutrient availability, and thermal stratification [N4-F3], further supporting a downward gradient in impurity concentration and ecological relevance.

---

## 3. Ecological functions

Each ice layer affects the lake ecosystem differently, primarily by altering light penetration, gas exchange, nutrient cycling, and benthic processes.

### Light penetration and photosynthesis
Ice cover fundamentally changes the underwater light environment. The evidence states that lake ice blocks the water-air interface and alters thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-F3]. Dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM also affect light penetration and nutrient availability, which in turn affects primary production [N4-F3]. Surface ice has the clearest direct effect on light transmission, because it is closest to the atmosphere, whereas middle and bottom ice may reduce light further as it thickens and becomes more opaque [N4-R4][N4-F3]. This means surface ice is most important for photosynthesis, and deeper ice layers progressively limit light availability for phototrophs below.

### Gas exchange and oxygen dynamics
Ice cover is a major constraint on ventilation. The evidence says ice cover inhibits water-column ventilation and snow cover limits gas exchange [N5-R2]. Oxygen depletion is common in ice-covered lakes because ice blocks ventilation [N5-R2]. Surface ice acts as the main barrier to atmospheric gas exchange, while middle ice may influence internal gas transport within the ice matrix, and bottom ice may affect benthic respiration and the exchange of gases between sediment and water [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence is strongest on the general constraint of ice on ventilation, but it does not provide a detailed layer-by-layer breakdown of oxygen flux [N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Nutrient cycling and benthic processes
Ice cover can concentrate nutrients in the under-ice water column. One source reports that seasonal ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. Another source says ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Bottom ice is especially relevant to benthic processes because it can interact with the sediment and influence nutrient fluxes from sediment to water [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Middle ice may also contribute indirectly by trapping liquid water and particulates, which can affect nutrient availability and microbial activity [N2-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, nutrient cycling is most directly linked to bottom ice, but all ice layers collectively shape nutrient availability and benthic activity [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 4. Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context

### Seasonal timing and environmental controls
Ice formation and melting are strongly governed by seasonal timing and environmental controls. The evidence notes that ice phenology—the timing of ice formation and melting—directly affects lake temperatures, seasonal stratification, and lake ecology [N6-R2]. Climate change is also reshaping ice dynamics, with warming causing earlier ice-off and later ice-on [N6-R4]. Wind is another key control: stronger winds can produce a deeper cold layer before ice-on, whereas calmer lakes have shallower cold layers [N6-F2]. This means seasonal dynamics are not uniform; they vary with local meteorological conditions and lake setting [N6-F2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Lake size, depth, and location
Lake size, depth, and location shape ice layer properties. Larger lakes tend to experience stronger winds than nearby smaller lakes, which affects the cold-layer depth before ice-on [N6-F2]. In deeper lakes, inverse stratification can form with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. Location also matters: boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes generally having longer ice duration and thicker ice [N4-F3]. This regional variation means that ice layer properties are not only a function of lake size and depth, but also of latitude and climate [N4-F3][N5-R4].

### Interaction with the water column and sediment
Ice layers interact with the water column through thermal stratification, nutrient cycling, and biogeochemical retention [N4-R4][N4-R3]. Bottom ice, in particular, can interact with the sediment because it may trap liquid water near the surface and be influenced by sediment-derived material [N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that ice influences internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing, which means ice layers can affect both the water column and the sediment interface [N6-F2][N4-R4]. This interaction is especially important for benthic processes and nutrient cycling [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 5. Terminology and layer boundaries

Standard terminology for surface, middle, and bottom ice is based on primary, congelation, and superimposed ice [N1-R2][N7-R1]. Primary ice is the first-formed layer, congelation ice forms as the ice thickens from below, and superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The boundary between layers is therefore defined by the freezing process rather than a fixed depth [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Superimposed ice can be thin and variable, forming when water flows onto the surface of primary ice or onto snow-covered ice [N7-R5]. This means the terminology is flexible and can vary by lake type and ice thickness [N4-F3][N6-F2][N7-R5].

Terminology differs by lake type and ice thickness because different lakes produce different ice forms and layering patterns. Boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes often having thicker ice and longer ice cover than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. Larger lakes may have stronger winds and deeper cold layers before ice-on, which affects the thermal profile and ice formation [N6-F2]. Thicker ice can host superimposed layers and trapped liquid pockets, whereas thinner ice may have a simpler structure dominated by primary and congelation ice [N7-R5][N2-R3]. Thus, terminology is not universal; it adapts to the physical and climatic conditions of each lake [N1-R2][N7-R1][N4-F3].

---

## Conclusion

In seasonally ice-covered lakes, surface ice, middle ice, and bottom ice are differentiated by:

- **Composition and structure**: surface ice is first-formed and closest to the atmosphere; middle ice is intermediate and may contain trapped water; bottom ice is deepest and often richest in particulate and labile organic matter [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F3].
- **Impurity content**: impurities tend to concentrate downward, with particulate and labile material retained in ice while other dissolved compounds are often excluded [N4-F3].
- **Ecological functions**: surface ice controls light and gas exchange; middle ice mediates internal transport and nutrient retention; bottom ice links the water column to sediment and benthic processes [N4-R4][N5-R2][N4-R3].
- **Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context**: ice formation is controlled by phenology, wind, thermal stratification, lake size, depth, and location; thicker or deeper lakes may have more complex ice-layer interactions [N6-R2][N6-F2][N4-F3][N2-R2].
- **Terminology and boundaries**: the standard classification is primary, congelation, and superimposed ice, with boundaries defined by freezing processes and ice type rather than fixed depths [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Taken together, these layers form a dynamic and ecologically significant ice system, in which each layer contributes to the overall function of the lake during winter [N4-R4][N5-R2][N6-R2][N4-F3].

## Integrated final answer: How surface, middle, and bottom ice differ in seasonally ice-covered lakes

Seasonally ice-covered lakes are stratified by ice in three main layers—surface, middle, and bottom—which differ in composition, impurity content, ecological function, seasonal dynamics, and lake-specific context. The evidence supports a layered structure rooted in ice formation processes, with terminology and boundaries shaped by freezing mechanisms and lake conditions [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Below I synthesize these differences across composition, impurity content, ecological functions, seasonal dynamics, and terminology.

---

## 1. Composition and formation depth

### Surface ice
Surface ice is the first-formed layer and is composed of primary ice and congelation ice in the standard classification of seasonally ice-covered lakes [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is formed at the water-air interface and is closest to atmospheric inputs, which makes it the layer most directly influenced by wind, temperature, and snow accumulation [N6-F2][N7-R5]. The evidence suggests that surface ice can be relatively pure in crystal structure, especially when it forms on calm water surfaces [N2-R1]. However, because it is the outermost layer, it may also incorporate snow and atmospheric impurities [N2-R1][N7-R5].

### Middle ice
Middle ice lies beneath the surface layer and is part of the same stratified ice structure [N1-R2]. It is described in the evidence as consisting mainly of primary ice on calm water surfaces and upper congelation ice [N2-R1]. This places it between the surface and the deeper ice, where the influence of atmospheric inputs diminishes but thermal and hydrodynamic effects remain strong [N6-F2]. The evidence also indicates that middle ice can be heterogeneous, because trapped liquid water layers can form near the surface and be incorporated into the ice matrix [N2-R3]. This suggests that middle ice may contain suspended materials or interstitial water, which can alter its composition relative to surface ice [N2-R3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice is the deepest static layer in the standard classification and is formed after the upper layers have developed [N1-R2][N2-R1]. It is the layer most directly connected to the water column below and, in some contexts, to the sediment [N4-R3][N2-R3]. The evidence points to bottom ice as being part of a broader stratified ice structure, where congelation and superimposed ice can coexist [N7-R5]. In deeper lakes, bottom ice may also form under inverse stratification, with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. This means bottom ice is not simply a “lower” layer but one that forms in response to thermal and hydrodynamic conditions below the ice surface [N2-R2][N6-F2].

---

## 2. Impurity content and concentration gradients

The impurity content of the ice layers is shaped by what is retained or excluded during freezing. The evidence shows that lake ice can store substantial organic matter, including particulate materials and dissolved labile compounds, while excluding many dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies a downward concentration gradient in impurities: particulate and labile material tends to accumulate in ice, whereas other dissolved materials may be filtered out [N4-F3].

### Surface ice
Surface ice may contain some atmospheric or snow-derived impurities, but the evidence does not provide a direct quantitative comparison of impurity levels relative to other layers. It does indicate that surface ice is formed by the water-air interface and therefore has direct access to atmospheric inputs [N2-R1][N7-R5]. This makes it the layer most likely to include snow-derived particulates and atmospheric tracers.

### Middle ice
Middle ice is likely to retain a mix of impurities, including some particulates and labile dissolved compounds, because it forms under the surface layer and can incorporate trapped water and suspended material [N2-R3][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that middle ice may contain upper congelation ice, which may have different impurity characteristics from surface ice [N2-R1]. Overall, middle ice appears to be an intermediate layer in impurity concentration, sitting between surface ice and bottom ice [N4-F3].

### Bottom ice
Bottom ice appears to be the richest in particulate and labile organic matter among the three layers [N4-F3]. The evidence reports that boreal lake ice has higher particulate carbon, chlorophyll-a, and protein-like dissolved compounds than underlying water, with ice retaining particulate material while excluding some dissolved compounds [N4-F3]. This implies that bottom ice can accumulate organic matter and biogenic material from the water column below, making it a significant reservoir of impurities [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM affect light penetration, nutrient availability, and thermal stratification [N4-F3], further supporting a downward gradient in impurity concentration and ecological relevance.

---

## 3. Ecological functions

Each ice layer affects the lake ecosystem differently, primarily by altering light penetration, gas exchange, nutrient cycling, and benthic processes.

### Light penetration and photosynthesis
Ice cover fundamentally changes the underwater light environment. The evidence states that lake ice blocks the water-air interface and alters thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-F3]. Dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM also affect light penetration and nutrient availability, which in turn affects primary production [N4-F3]. Surface ice has the clearest direct effect on light transmission, because it is closest to the atmosphere, whereas middle and bottom ice may reduce light further as it thickens and becomes more opaque [N4-R4][N4-F3]. This means surface ice is most important for photosynthesis, and deeper ice layers progressively limit light availability for phototrophs below.

### Gas exchange and oxygen dynamics
Ice cover is a major constraint on ventilation. The evidence says ice cover inhibits water-column ventilation and snow cover limits gas exchange [N5-R2]. Oxygen depletion is common in ice-covered lakes because ice blocks ventilation [N5-R2]. Surface ice acts as the main barrier to atmospheric gas exchange, while middle ice may influence internal gas transport within the ice matrix, and bottom ice may affect benthic respiration and the exchange of gases between sediment and water [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence is strongest on the general constraint of ice on ventilation, but it does not provide a detailed layer-by-layer breakdown of oxygen flux [N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Nutrient cycling and benthic processes
Ice cover can concentrate nutrients in the under-ice water column. One source reports that seasonal ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. Another source says ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Bottom ice is especially relevant to benthic processes because it can interact with the sediment and influence nutrient fluxes from sediment to water [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Middle ice may also contribute indirectly by trapping liquid water and particulates, which can affect nutrient availability and microbial activity [N2-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, nutrient cycling is most directly linked to bottom ice, but all ice layers collectively shape nutrient availability and benthic activity [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 4. Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context

### Seasonal timing and environmental controls
Ice formation and melting are strongly governed by seasonal timing and environmental controls. The evidence notes that ice phenology—the timing of ice formation and melting—directly affects lake temperatures, seasonal stratification, and lake ecology [N6-R2]. Climate change is also reshaping ice dynamics, with warming causing earlier ice-off and later ice-on [N6-R4]. Wind is another key control: stronger winds can produce a deeper cold layer before ice-on, whereas calmer lakes have shallower cold layers [N6-F2]. This means seasonal dynamics are not uniform; they vary with local meteorological conditions and lake setting [N6-F2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Lake size, depth, and location
Lake size, depth, and location shape ice layer properties. Larger lakes tend to experience stronger winds than nearby smaller lakes, which affects the cold-layer depth before ice-on [N6-F2]. In deeper lakes, inverse stratification can form with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. Location also matters: boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes generally having longer ice duration and thicker ice [N4-F3]. This regional variation means that ice layer properties are not only a function of lake size and depth, but also of latitude and climate [N4-F3][N5-R4].

### Interaction with the water column and sediment
Ice layers interact with the water column through thermal stratification, nutrient cycling, and biogeochemical retention [N4-R4][N4-R3]. Bottom ice, in particular, can interact with the sediment because it may trap liquid water near the surface and be influenced by sediment-derived material [N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that ice influences internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing, which means ice layers can affect both the water column and the sediment interface [N6-F2][N4-R4]. This interaction is especially important for benthic processes and nutrient cycling [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 5. Terminology and layer boundaries

Standard terminology for surface, middle, and bottom ice is based on primary, congelation, and superimposed ice [N1-R2][N7-R1]. Primary ice is the first-formed layer, congelation ice forms as the ice thickens from below, and superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The boundary between layers is therefore defined by the freezing process rather than a fixed depth [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Superimposed ice can be thin and variable, forming when water flows onto the surface of primary ice or onto snow-covered ice [N7-R5]. This means the terminology is flexible and can vary by lake type and ice thickness [N4-F3][N6-F2][N7-R5].

Terminology differs by lake type and ice thickness because different lakes produce different ice forms and layering patterns. Boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes often having thicker ice and longer ice cover than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. Larger lakes may have stronger winds and deeper cold layers before ice-on, which affects the thermal profile and ice formation [N6-F2]. Thicker ice can host superimposed layers and trapped liquid pockets, whereas thinner ice may have a simpler structure dominated by primary and congelation ice [N7-R5][N2-R3]. Thus, terminology is not universal; it adapts to the physical and climatic conditions of each lake [N1-R2][N7-R1][N4-F3].

---

## Conclusion

In seasonally ice-covered lakes, surface ice, middle ice, and bottom ice are differentiated by:

- **Composition and structure**: surface ice is first-formed and closest to the atmosphere; middle ice is intermediate and may contain trapped water; bottom ice is deepest and often richest in particulate and labile organic matter [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F3].
- **Impurity content**: impurities tend to concentrate downward, with particulate and labile material retained in ice while other dissolved compounds are often excluded [N4-F3].
- **Ecological functions**: surface ice controls light and gas exchange; middle ice mediates internal transport and nutrient retention; bottom ice links the water column to sediment and benthic processes [N4-R4][N5-R2][N4-R3].
- **Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context**: ice formation is controlled by phenology, wind, thermal stratification, lake size, depth, and location; thicker or deeper lakes may have more complex ice-layer interactions [N6-R2][N6-F2][N4-F3][N2-R2].
- **Terminology and boundaries**: the standard classification is primary, congelation, and superimposed ice, with boundaries defined by freezing processes and ice type rather than fixed depths [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Taken together, these layers form a dynamic and ecologically significant ice system, in which each layer contributes to the overall function of the lake during winter [N4-R4][N5-R2][N6-R2][N4-F3].

The evidence also notes that dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM affect light penetration, nutrient availability, and thermal stratification [N4-F3], further supporting a downward gradient in impurity concentration and ecological relevance.

---

## 3. Ecological functions

Each ice layer affects the lake ecosystem differently, primarily by altering light penetration, gas exchange, nutrient cycling, and benthic processes.

### Light penetration and photosynthesis
Ice cover fundamentally changes the underwater light environment. The evidence states that lake ice blocks the water-air interface and alters thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms and food webs [N4-F3]. Dissolved organic carbon and colored DOM also affect light penetration and nutrient availability, which in turn affects primary production [N4-F3]. Surface ice has the clearest direct effect on light transmission, because it is closest to the atmosphere, whereas middle and bottom ice may reduce light further as it thickens and becomes more opaque [N4-R4][N4-F3]. This means surface ice is most important for photosynthesis, and deeper ice layers progressively limit light availability for phototrophs below.

### Gas exchange and oxygen dynamics
Ice cover is a major constraint on ventilation. The evidence says ice cover inhibits water-column ventilation and snow cover limits gas exchange [N5-R2]. Oxygen depletion is common in ice-covered lakes because ice blocks ventilation [N5-R2]. Surface ice acts as the main barrier to atmospheric gas exchange, while middle ice may influence internal gas transport within the ice matrix, and bottom ice may affect benthic respiration and the exchange of gases between sediment and water [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence is strongest on the general constraint of ice on ventilation, but it does not provide a detailed layer-by-layer breakdown of oxygen flux [N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Nutrient cycling and benthic processes
Ice cover can concentrate nutrients in the under-ice water column. One source reports that seasonal ice cover can reduce the volume of liquid water in a lake and significantly increase under-ice nutrient concentration [N4-R3]. Another source says ice cover reorganizes lake ecosystems by altering thermal stratification and solar radiation, creating conditions that support different organisms, food webs, and biogeochemical processes [N4-R4]. Bottom ice is especially relevant to benthic processes because it can interact with the sediment and influence nutrient fluxes from sediment to water [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Middle ice may also contribute indirectly by trapping liquid water and particulates, which can affect nutrient availability and microbial activity [N2-R3][N4-F3]. Overall, nutrient cycling is most directly linked to bottom ice, but all ice layers collectively shape nutrient availability and benthic activity [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 4. Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context

### Seasonal timing and environmental controls
Ice formation and melting are strongly governed by seasonal timing and environmental controls. The evidence notes that ice phenology—the timing of ice formation and melting—directly affects lake temperatures, seasonal stratification, and lake ecology [N6-R2]. Climate change is also reshaping ice dynamics, with warming causing earlier ice-off and later ice-on [N6-R4]. Wind is another key control: stronger winds can produce a deeper cold layer before ice-on, whereas calmer lakes have shallower cold layers [N6-F2]. This means seasonal dynamics are not uniform; they vary with local meteorological conditions and lake setting [N6-F2][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Lake size, depth, and location
Lake size, depth, and location shape ice layer properties. Larger lakes tend to experience stronger winds than nearby smaller lakes, which affects the cold-layer depth before ice-on [N6-F2]. In deeper lakes, inverse stratification can form with a thin buoyant layer of cold water near 0°C below the ice [N2-R2]. Location also matters: boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes generally having longer ice duration and thicker ice [N4-F3]. This regional variation means that ice layer properties are not only a function of lake size and depth, but also of latitude and climate [N4-F3][N5-R4].

### Interaction with the water column and sediment
Ice layers interact with the water column through thermal stratification, nutrient cycling, and biogeochemical retention [N4-R4][N4-R3]. Bottom ice, in particular, can interact with the sediment because it may trap liquid water near the surface and be influenced by sediment-derived material [N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that ice influences internal waves, circulation, and vertical mixing, which means ice layers can affect both the water column and the sediment interface [N6-F2][N4-R4]. This interaction is especially important for benthic processes and nutrient cycling [N4-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 5. Terminology and layer boundaries

Standard terminology for surface, middle, and bottom ice is based on primary, congelation, and superimposed ice [N1-R2][N7-R1]. Primary ice is the first-formed layer, congelation ice forms as the ice thickens from below, and superimposed ice forms on top of primary ice [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The boundary between layers is therefore defined by the freezing process rather than a fixed depth [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5]. Superimposed ice can be thin and variable, forming when water flows onto the surface of primary ice or onto snow-covered ice [N7-R5]. This means the terminology is flexible and can vary by lake type and ice thickness [N4-F3][N6-F2][N7-R5].

Terminology differs by lake type and ice thickness because different lakes produce different ice forms and layering patterns. Boreal and Arctic lakes differ in ice duration, thickness, and quality, with Arctic lakes often having thicker ice and longer ice cover than boreal lakes [N4-F3]. Larger lakes may have stronger winds and deeper cold layers before ice-on, which affects the thermal profile and ice formation [N6-F2]. Thicker ice can host superimposed layers and trapped liquid pockets, whereas thinner ice may have a simpler structure dominated by primary and congelation ice [N7-R5][N2-R3]. Thus, terminology is not universal; it adapts to the physical and climatic conditions of each lake [N1-R2][N7-R1][N4-F3].

---

## Conclusion

In seasonally ice-covered lakes, surface ice, middle ice, and bottom ice are differentiated by:

- **Composition and structure**: surface ice is first-formed and closest to the atmosphere; middle ice is intermediate and may contain trapped water; bottom ice is deepest and often richest in particulate and labile organic matter [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F3].
- **Impurity content**: impurities tend to concentrate downward, with particulate and labile material retained in ice while other dissolved compounds are often excluded [N4-F3].
- **Ecological functions**: surface ice controls light and gas exchange; middle ice mediates internal transport and nutrient retention; bottom ice links the water column to sediment and benthic processes [N4-R4][N5-R2][N4-R3].
- **Seasonal dynamics and lake-specific context**: ice formation is controlled by phenology, wind, thermal stratification, lake size, depth, and location; thicker or deeper lakes may have more complex ice-layer interactions [N6-R2][N6-F2][N4-F3][N2-R2].
- **Terminology and boundaries**: the standard classification is primary, congelation, and superimposed ice, with boundaries defined by freezing processes and ice type rather than fixed depths [N1-R2][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Taken together, these layers form a dynamic and ecologically significant ice system, in which each layer contributes to the overall function of the lake during winter [N4-R4][N5-R2][N6-R2][N4-F3].
